title: A king on a donkey (Luke 19:28–40)
hookLine: crowds wave branches and throw coats on the road for a man on a borrowed donkey

lines: A COLT NO ONE HAS RIDDEN.
THE LORD HATH NEED OF HIM.
cards: Motorcades, tinted windows, security in dark suits, a red carpet: that's how power tends to arrive. This arrival starts on the road over the Mount of Olives, with Jerusalem filling up for Passover.

Jesus sends two disciples ahead to a village with strange instructions: you'll find a colt tied up that no one has ever ridden; untie it and bring it, and if anyone asks why, say: "The Lord hath need of him."
It's exactly as he said: the owners ask, the disciples answer, the owners let it go. A borrowed donkey.

teach.b: They throw their coats over the colt and set Jesus on it. As he rides, people spread their coats on the road, a red carpet made of whatever they're wearing.

Coming down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his followers shouts, in Luke's words in the King James Bible: "Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest."
Luke doesn't use today's word, but Matthew, Mark and John do. In Matthew the crowd shouts: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest."
Hosanna comes from Hebrew, hoshia na: save, please. It comes from Psalm 118, the psalm the crowd is quoting, where the King James renders it: "Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD."
Over time it became a shout of praise, but underneath it's a cry for help: save us, now. John adds the palm branches, which is why churches call this Palm Sunday.

teach.h: A DONKEY, NOT A WAR HORSE.
teach.b: Why a donkey? The prophet Zechariah had said Jerusalem's king would come "lowly, and riding upon an ass." In the next verse the horse is cut off from Jerusalem, and the king speaks peace.
No emperor would arrive like this. Some Pharisees tell him to quiet his followers.
He says: "I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out."

teach.h: BLESSED BE THE KING THAT COMETH.
teach.b: Christians still shout hosanna in worship. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans and others sing it in the communion prayers, before the bread and cup are shared.

how: Many churches keep Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week, with palm branches, a procession and readings of the entry into Jerusalem. In many churches the Sanctus, sung in the communion prayers, ends with Hosanna in the highest.

games.q: you're one of the disciples. Jesus sends you to untie a colt in a village. its owners ask, why are you untying it? what do you say?
o: the Lord hath need of him.
say nothing and lead it away.
games.why: they say what he told them to: the Lord hath need of him. and the owners let it go.

practice: The crowd laid down their coats, the thing they had on them, so someone else's way would be smoother.

Think of one person whose road could use smoothing, and what you could lay down for them: your turn to talk, your plan, your seat, an hour, your need to be right. If you pray, you can say the old word, hosanna: save, please.

wordCard.voice: Hosanna. From the Hebrew hoshia na: save, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung for a king on a donkey.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. The Greek Gospels carried it over as hosanna.

carryVoice: Your line: the stones would cry out. Tomorrow, tables go over in the temple. Day sixty-one, complete.
